newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmen oil tender hinges on end to Caspian row.
newsitem.headline: Turkmen oil tender hinges on end to Caspian row.

text.p: A tender to develop big energy reserves in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea will not proceed until a row over ownership of the Caspian's resources is settled, Turkmenistan's oil and gas minister said on Wednesday.
But Gochmurad Nazdzhanov also told an international projects conference he was confident the row would be settled this year.
"The tender will depend on an agreement over the division of Caspian Sea territory," Nazdzhanov told Reuters at the conference. "But I think the tender will go ahead this year."
It had been originally planned for early this year.
Nazdzhanov said the sale had attracted interest from major international oil groups, although no deals had been signed yet.
He said Exxon Corp, Mobil Corp, Agip SpA, Unocal Corp and Royal Dutch/Shell Group had all expressed interest.
"The Caspian Shelf is our major hope," he said in a speech to the second Turkmenistan International Oil and Gas 1997 Projects Conference.
The tender will be for around six blocks on the Caspian shelf, which Nazdzhanov said contained about 300 million tonnes of crude oil.
Turkmenistan's total offshore territory holds an estimated 2.5 billion tonnes of oil, officials have said.
But potential investors are keen to see a territorial row among countries surrounding the energy-rich Caspian resolved before proceeding with big-ticket investments.
Russia and Iran have argued that the sea is really a lake and is the common property of all the states surrounding it.
Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan say the Caspian is a sea and should be divided up into sectors and exploited by each country as such.

The issue of who can claim ownership to the Caspian's vast oil resources, which rank eighth in the world in terms of discovered reserves, is making potential investors nervous and could delay development of Turkmenistan's offshore resources.

Alan Weatherill of Shell EP International Ventures B.V., part of the Royal Dutch/Shell group and a potential investor in Turkmenistan's offshore resources, said a settlement to the row over ownership of Caspian reserves was crucial for the company.
"We don't actually have a deal lined up," he said. "But we definitely want this row settled, just because we want to know who we will be talking to," he said.
Recent Turkmen claims to some Azeri oilfields, including some already under development, further complicate the issue.

Turkmenistan said in January that the Azeri oilfield and part of the Chirag field -- both in the sector of the Caspian claimed by Azerbaijan and under development by a multinational consortium -- belonged to Turkmenistan.
Azerbaijan, with fields already under development by the $8-billion Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC) consortium, rejected the claim, but the row continues to simmer.
But some executives said that that particular quarrel should not affect output at existing projects.
"I'm confident that somehow any disagreements about lines will be settled in a way that will allow oil production to continue," said John Imle, President of Unocal, which is part of the AIOC project.

Nazdzhanov said Turkmenistan's gas reserves were estimated at 21.0 trillion cubic metres and oil reserves at 6.5 to 7.0 billion tonnes. But production has slipped in recent years as production infrastructure aged.
He forecast Turkmen oil output to rise to 14 million tonnes (280,000 barrels per day) by the year 2000 from 1996 output of around 110,000 bpd.
